sentences.text: 1 1. Briefly stated, the case of the prosecution is that the complainant Rajpal has a house of two and a half floors at no. C- 237, Gali No. 1, Pratap Nagar, Delhi.
He used to reside on the ground floor whereas three tenants used to reside on the first floor and another tenant used to reside on the top floor.

It is alleged that on 09.05.2010 at about 09:30 AM, while the complainant was sitting outside his house, his daughter came and informed him that a gas cylinder has caught fire in the house of accused Subodh, who was his tenant.
He rushed to the house of the accused and found that his wife was inside the room and the gas cylinder was on fire.
They tried to put out the fire but suddenly an explosion occurred in the cylinder, due to which the walls of the room got damaged, which also damaged the neighbouring houses.
As a result, the victim Harpal, who was the neighbour of the complainant, lost his life and other persons suffered grievous and simple injuries.
The allegations of the prosecution are that due to negligence in taking care of the cylinder, the incident occurred.

As such, it is alleged that the accused has committed the offences punishable under Section 285/337/338/304A of Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter, "IPC"), for which FIR No. 86/2010 was registered at the Harsh Vihar Police Station, New Delhi.

10. I have heard the learned APP for the State and learned counsel for the accused at length.

11. It is argued by the learned APP for the State that all the ingredients of the offence are fulfilled in the present case.
He has argued that the factum of incident is proved.
Further, the injured and eye-witnesses have deposed about the incident in detail and the other documentary evidence on record has corroborated the version of the prosecution witnesses.

ANALYSIS - 13.

The accused has been charged for the offences of negligent conduct with fire or combustible matter (S. 285 IPC), causing grievous hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others (S.
337 IPC), causing hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others (S. 338 IPC), and causing death by a rash or negligent act (S. 304A IPC) in the present case.
The prosecution has to prove that the accused did an act so rashly or negligently with respect to fire or combustible matter in his possession so as to endanger human life etc.
Under Section 337/338/304A IPC, hurt and death of the victim should be caused in pursuance of such rash or negligent act of the accused.
14. Thus, the gravamen of the offences under Section 285/337/338/304A IPC is the act of the accused, done with "rashness" or "negligence".
The IPC does not define either of these terms.
However, the ambit of these terms has now been settled by judicial pronouncements of superior Courts.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rathnashalvan vs. State of Karnataka (2007) 3 SCC 474 has observed, inter alia, as under-:
"7. .... Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper care and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.

sentences.text: Rashness means doing an act with the consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.
Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors.

A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of care and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.

Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.
8. As noted above, "rashness" consists in hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so, and that it may cause injury.
The criminality lies in such a case in running the risk of doing such an act with recklessness or indifference as to the consequences.

Criminal negligence on the other hand, is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which,
having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge has arisen it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted."
Similar observations were made by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sushil Ansal vs. CBI (2014) 6 SCC 173.

The standard of negligence was discussed in the said case, by observing, inter alia,
as under-:
"58.

In the case of "negligence" the courts have favoured a meaning which implies a gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual DEV
CHAUDHARY CHAUDHARY Date: 2023.08.21 15:29:46 +0530 which having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge arises, it may be the imperative duty of the accused to have adopted.

Negligence has been understood to be an omission to do something which a reasonable man guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person would not do.

Unlike rashness, where the imputability arises from acting despite the consciousness,
negligence implies acting without such consciousness, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him.

The imputability in the case of negligence arises from the neglect of the civil duty of State vs . on 21 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/68747838/
5 circumspection."
Thus, rashness implies doing an act despite the consciousness that it might result in injuries.
Negligence, on the other hand, means lack of reasonable care that a person placed is the fact situation ought to take, in order to avoid injuries.
15. Needless to mention, in criminal law, the burden of proof on the prosecution is that of beyond reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by adducing cogent evidence that points towards the guilt of the accused.
The evidence in the present case is to be weighed keeping in view the above legal standards.

PW 2/A of the complainant Rajpal, wherein it is mentioned that on the date of incident, he was sitting outside his house, when his daughter Baby came and informed him that a gas cylinder in the room of the accused has caught fire.
The witness has narrated about the incident and has stated that on ac- count of the explosion, several persons, including his wife and his daughter got injured.
In his statement Ex. PW2/A, forming basis of the FIR, the complainant has stated that the incident took place due DEV

There is no ex- planation on record as to what investigation was done qua the wife of the accused and why the charge-sheet was then filed against the accused and not his wife.
17. Moving forward, the prosecution has examined four in- jured persons apart from the complainant during the trial.
PW1 Baby has only stated that she heard noise coming from the upper floor of their house and her parents had tried to extinguish the fire, after which an explosion took place.
She has stated that the wife of the accused was present in the room of the accused, when the blast occurred.
The testimony of this witness is of no help to the prosecu- tion as she has not deposed about either the role of the accused or the incident in detail.
18. Similarly, the complainant Rajpal (PW2) has also de- posed about the incident.
However, he has also not deposed about the role of the accused in the incident.
Pertinently, the complainant PW2 has not stated that his daughter Baby had informed him about the fire in the cylinder.
During his deposition, he has stated that the wife of the accused had come from the first floor and had raised an alarm regarding the fire.
He has named the wife of the accused as Reena.
However, in the complaint Ex. PW2/A, the name of the wife of the accused is mentioned as Aruna.
19. Further, PW2 has stated that the wife of the accused in- formed him that she was preparing food and when he went to the first floor, he saw that the gas cylinder was on fire.

Apart from the witnesses mentioned above, there is no that witness to either the incident or to depose about the role of the accused.
The prosecution has cited no other independent witnesses to the crime.
The other police witnesses and doctors are only relev- ant to prove the investigation and the nature of injuries.
Therefore, no witness has been brought to the stand by the prosecution to either prove that the accused had purchased the cylinder, or that the cylin- der was found in possession of the accused.
Further, there is no wit- ness to the effect that the accused had committed any rash or negli- gent act by purchasing the cylinder or pursuant thereto.
Further, on the date of incident, the role of the accused is also not specified.
It is an admitted case of the prosecution witnesses that the accused was not present at his house, on the date of incident.
Therefore, there is no evidence on record whatsoever to point towards the role of the accused in the alleged crime.

As noted above, the initial case of the prosecution was against the wife of the accused and thereafter,
the chargesheet has been filed against the accused without giving any cogent grounds regarding his involvement.

sentences.text: In this regard, the first IO in the present matter is PW5 SI Jai Bhag- wan, who was questioned by the court during his examination.

A question was put to the witness as to why he did not record the state- ment of the victim Yashodha,
whose medical was conducted on the date of incident.
His explanation is that the recording of statement skipped his mind.
It is clear that an absurd explanation is given by the IO in this regard.
He failed to record the statement of the injured in a case based on the bodily injuries.
24. Further, the IO has failed to investigate crucial points in the present matter.
In his cross-examination, he has specifically ad- mitted that the fire was extinguished by the fire tenders on the spot.
However, he admitted that he did not record statement of any fire men in the present matter.

Further, with regard to the cylinder, he stated that he did not seize any receipt or document to show that the accused had either purchased or received delivery of the said cylin- der.
25.
As such, in the whole case of the prosecution, there is no evidence to point towards the fact that the accused was owner of the cylinder.

In this regard, it is also relevant to note at this juncture that as per the seizure memo of the cylinder that is Ex. PW2/B, the cylinder was seized on 10.09.2010,
which is after about four months from the date of incident.
There is no cogent explanation in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses as to why there was inordin- ate delay in seizure of the case property.
Further, the first IO PW5 has specifically admitted in his cross-examination that he did not send the gas cylinder for expert examination to the BIS.
The second DEV CHAUDHARY CHAUDHARY Date: 2023.08.21 15:30:24 +0530
IO SI Pratap Singh had expired during the trial and as such, he could not be examined.
26. However, the accused has admitted the examination re- port of the BIS in his statement recorded under section 294 CrPC.
In the document Ex. A1, an opinion was sought from the Bureau of In- dian Standards (BIS) regarding the cylinder seized by the IO.
As per the report dated 28.01.2011, it is opined that the gas cylinder did not have any ISI mark or other details of the oil company.
There were no details of the manufacturer, and the valve of the cylinder also did not have any marking.

The report concludes that the cylinder is spurious and does not have any ISI or BIS standard mark, and as such, it is not certified by the BIS.
27.
However, in the considered opinion of this Court, apart from the said report, which is in nature of an expert opinion, there is no other evidence on record.
It is already noted above that the prosecution has failed to link the cylinder to the present accused in the case.
Therefore, mere fact that the cylinder was spurious is not sufficient to impute any liability to the accused.

In this regard,
the the fact that the negligence of the accused was a proximate result of the injury/death has to be established by the prosecution to prove its case under Section 337/337/338/304A IPC.
There is no evidence on record to link the injuries directly and effectively to the act or omission of the accused.
Therefore, the prosecution has failed to prove as to the what exactly was the neglect of the accused.
Was the incident caused solely on account of any rash and negligent act of the accused, is a question which remains unanswered.
At this stage, the doctrine of causa causans is to be referred.

The Hon'ble DEV CHAUDHARY CHAUDHARY Date:

sentences.text:
As to what is meant by causa causans we may gainfully refer to Black's Law Dictionary (5th Edn.) which defines that expression as under:
"Causa causans.--The immediate cause; the last link in the chain of causation."
The Advance Law Lexicon edited by Justice Chandrachud, former Chief Justice of India defines causa causans as follows:
"Causa causans.--The immediate cause as opposed to a remote cause; the 'last link in the chain of causation'; the real effective cause of damage."

Therefore, the act or omission of the accused must be linked directly with the injury caused and the act or omission attributed to the accused must be the causa causans and not merely causa sine qua non.
As such, without any ocular or documentary evidence to prove the same, the prosecution has failed to discharge its onus.
28. The fact that the cylinder was spurious may or may not have been the ultimate reason for the blast in the cylinder.

There- fore, it is evident that the prosecution has failed to produce any co- gent evidence on record to prove that the act of the accused was rash and negligent, and the said act led to the explosion in the cylinder, which ultimately led to a tragic death and many injuries.
29. Moreover, there are other circumstances on record, which throw a doubt on the testimony of the prosecution witnesses.
The IO PW5 has stated that the site plan Ex. PW5/B was prepared at the instance of the complainant.
However, the complainant PW2 has not deposed that he had signed the site plan.
Further, the document DEV CHAUDHARY CHAUDHARY Date: 2023.08.21 15:30:38 +0530 does not bear the signature of the complainant.
Moving forward, there is discrepancy in the deposition of the witnesses regarding the tenants.
The IO has stated that the deceased Harpal was one of the tenants' of the complainant.
However, the complainant has stated that the deceased was his neighbour.
Further, no investigation has been done from the PCR van and no statements of public witnesses were recorded by the IO.
No other witness of the locality was pro- duced in the stand by the IO.
Further, there is no explanation as to who had clicked the photographs of the spot.
No witness has de- posed about the same.
As such, in my opinion, the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the case against the accused.

The fact that the victims suffered injuries on account of blast in the cylinder, even if proved, does not ipso facto prove that the explosion took place on account of negligence or rashness imputable to the accused.
CONCLUSION - 30.

To recapitulate the above discussion, in the present matter, it was incumbent upon the prosecution, to prove that on ac- count of rashness and negligence of the accused Subodh, an explo- sion took place in the gas cylinder, and as such, due to his act, the victims suffered injuries and one State vs .

on 21 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/68747838/
9 of the victim lost his life.
Even after appreciating the testimony of all the injured persons, there is nothing on record to link the accused with the offence.
The shoddy investigation done by the IO only weakens the case of the prosecu- tion.
As such, this court has no hesitation to hold that the prosecu- tion has failed to prove the offence at the required threshold.

31. Resultantly, the accused SUBODH son of Mahesh is DEV CHAUDHARY CHAUDHARY Date:
2023.08.21 15:30:46 +0530 hereby found not guilty.
He is hereby ACQUITTED of the offences under Section 285/337/338/304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

The accused has been charged for the offences of negligent conduct with fire or combustible matter (S. 285 IPC), causing grievous hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others (S.
337 IPC), causing hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others (S. 338 IPC), and causing death by a rash or negligent act (S. 304A IPC) in the present case.
The prosecution has to prove that the accused did an act so rashly or negligently with respect to fire or combustible matter in his possession so as to endanger human life etc.
Under Section 337/338/304A IPC, hurt and death of the victim should be caused in pursuance of such rash or negligent act of the accused.
14. Thus, the gravamen of the offences under Section 285/337/338/304A IPC is the act of the accused, done with "rashness" or "negligence".
The IPC does not define either of these terms.
However, the ambit of these terms has now been settled by judicial pronouncements of superior Courts.
Thus, rashness implies doing an act despite the consciousness that it might result in injuries.
Negligence, on the other hand, means lack of reasonable care that a person placed is the fact situation ought to take, in order to avoid injuries.
15. Needless to mention, in criminal law, the burden of proof on the prosecution is that of beyond reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by adducing cogent evidence that points towards the guilt of the accused.
Therefore, no witness has been brought to the stand by the prosecution to either prove that the accused had purchased the cylinder, or that the cylin- der was found in possession of the accused.
Further, there is no wit- ness to the effect that the accused had committed any rash or negli- gent act by purchasing the cylinder or pursuant thereto.
Further, on the date of incident, the role of the accused is also not specified.
It is an admitted case of the prosecution witnesses that the accused was not present at his house, on the date of incident.
Therefore, there is no evidence on record whatsoever to point towards the role of the accused in the alleged crime.
He failed to record the statement of the injured in a case based on the bodily injuries.
However, in the considered opinion of this Court, apart from the said report, which is in nature of an expert opinion, there is no other evidence on record.
Therefore, mere fact that the cylinder was spurious is not sufficient to impute any liability to the accused.
In this regard,
the the fact that the negligence of the accused was a proximate result of the injury/death has to be established by the prosecution to prove its case under Section 337/337/338/304A IPC.
There is no evidence on record to link the injuries directly and effectively to the act or omission of the accused.
Therefore, the prosecution has failed to prove as to the what exactly was the neglect of the accused.
Was the incident caused solely on account of any rash and negligent act of the accused, is a question which remains unanswered.
At this stage, the doctrine of causa causans is to be referred.
Therefore, the act or omission of the accused must be linked directly with the injury caused and the act or omission attributed to the accused must be the causa causans and not merely causa sine qua non.
As such, without any ocular or documentary evidence to prove the same, the prosecution has failed to discharge its onus.
There- fore, it is evident that the prosecution has failed to produce any co- gent evidence on record to prove that the act of the accused was rash and negligent, and the said act led to the explosion in the cylinder, which ultimately led to a tragic death and many injuries.
The fact that the victims suffered injuries on account of blast in the cylinder, even if proved, does not ipso facto prove that the explosion took place on account of negligence or rashness imputable to the accused.
To recapitulate the above discussion, in the present matter, it was incumbent upon the prosecution, to prove that on ac- count of rashness and negligence of the accused Subodh, an explo- sion took place in the gas cylinder, and as such, due to his act, the victims suffered injuries and one State vs .
Even after appreciating the testimony of all the injured persons, there is nothing on record to link the accused with the offence.
The shoddy investigation done by the IO only weakens the case of the prosecu- tion.
